reason: I attacked the page number first, because the verifier's own argument for it was bad. Saying the Internet Archive record shows only 74 scanned images so page 74 cannot hold it is not sound: image counts and printed page numbers are different things. But the record settles it anyway on better grounds. I pulled archive.org/metadata/cassandraessay0000nigh directly: title Cassandra: an essay, publisher Old Westbury NY Feminist Press, date 1979, isbn 091267055X, description 60 p, imagecount 74. Sixty printed pages, so there is no page 74 in the book at all, and the old citation was impossible rather than merely wrong. Page 25 is then positively corroborated and internally coherent: Landow's VictorianWeb essay quotes the sentence with (25) and calls it Cassandra's third paragraph, and cites two later passages from the same edition at (27) and (37), which is exactly the spacing you would get if the essay text opens near p. 25 after Stark's introduction and runs to p. 60. One caveat the note should not be blamed for: Landow's bibliography gives the edition as Cassandra, ed. Myra Stark, London: Feminist Press, n.d., without the place and year. The Internet Archive record supplies Old Westbury and 1979, and Stark's is the only Feminist Press edition, so the proposal's fuller imprint is a correction of Landow, not an invention. Wording: Landow elides the middle, quoting passion, intellect, moral activity . . . and a place in society, so his page does not by itself prove these three. It is nonetheless certain. The clause no one of the three is unintelligible without an antecedent three, and Nightingale writes the same triad plainly elsewhere in Cassandra: Passion, intellect, moral activity, these three have never been satisfied in a woman. The sentence is an English original with no translator, so this track's usual failure mode, translation drift, cannot arise, and every edition prints the same words. Only the dash setting is unverified at the page, spaced or closed, and that is typography, not wording. Attribution: Nightingale's own essay, in her own voice, not a character and not reported of her by another; not on the misattribution list. Scope: written 1852, privately printed 1860 in volume 2 of Suggestions for Thought, first published 1928 in Ray Strachey's The Cause, all pre-1999, and not scripture even though its epigraph plays on Mark. Publishability: a question, not a wound. Tag: Essay is the form, and the edition calls itself Cassandra: An Essay. Source line: 102 characters, leads with the name, no dash, no straight double quote, and names the editor where a translated line would name the translator.
